answers.question: (1) What free/cheap alternative covers the wedge?
answers.answer: Not newly verified: no search could run and the Printables, Etsy-listing and eBay-listing pages were refused. From the case file (earlier scan, agent_reported, not re-read by me): a free CC BY-SA Printables knob pack with an 8-step DIY route (E4, E6, E7) that covers the wedge only partially because the buyer must customise, print and glue; an Etsy 'replacement part from photo or drawing' service at $40 (E3); and an eBay seller of a model-specific 3D-printed Thermador knob at $60.00 already in 2016 (E2) against $289.95 for a used OEM knob (E1). The 2016 eBay item shows the model-specific printed-knob wedge pre-dates the entrant. Whether Etsy/eBay already list knobs by exact model number at or below $25 with fast shipping (the case file's own falsifier) is unchecked and is the first thing a human should look at.

answers.question: (2) What structural edge exists and who could copy it?
answers.answer: None that is exclusive. The only candidate is the accumulated catalog of fit-tested knob models by appliance model and part number; any rival with calipers and a printer can re-measure the same knob, and no licence, data source or supplier is exclusive to the entrant. Etsy's creativity standards (effective June 10, 2025) require 3D-printed items to be produced from the seller's own original design and restrict items made from other people's templates (D21, D22, D23). That removes template-remix sellers from Etsy but is open to any seller willing to do original CAD, so it is a shared tailwind, not an entrant edge; it also means the entrant cannot legally shortcut the catalog by remixing the free CC BY-SA pack for sale on Etsy. Falsifier: several sellers already listing knobs by exact model number at or below $25 with ship times of 3 days or less, or a median demand per model well below the break-even of about 0.3-0.45 orders per model per month.

answers.question: (3) Who demonstrably pays and how much?
answers.answer: Only the earlier-scan evidence, not re-read by me: a 2016 eBay feedback text shows a $60.00 3D-printed discontinued Thermador knob next to a $289.95 used OEM knob (E1, E2), and an Etsy custom-part service lists $40.00 with 4.9k reviews (E3). Nothing current was verified: today's price level, sold counts, repeat rate and per-SKU volume were not found. The case file's $15-25 price is the notes' own estimate, so $20 is an assumption.

answers.question: (4) Legal/platform constraints?
answers.answer: Etsy: 3D-printed items must be based on the seller's original design (D21) and the policy restricts items made from other people's templates (D22); the author of one seller post reads it as likely to remove shops that only use others' templates (D23). So every catalog entry must be the entrant's own CAD from measured parts, and the free CC BY-SA 4.0 knob pack (E7) can be used on Etsy only as reference, not remixed. Safety: Consumer Product Safety Act section 15(b) opens with 'Every manufacturer of a consumer product...' and, per the page, extends the duty to distributors and retailers who obtain information about a defect or risk (D24); a knob on a gas or electric range is heat-exposed and safety-relevant, so product-liability exposure exists and insurance cost was not found. Not verified: eBay/Etsy rules on gas-appliance control parts, OEM part-number and trademark use, eBay and Etsy current fee schedules.

answers.question: (5) Year-1 numbers?
answers.answer: All inputs are labelled assumptions except where noted; the decisive one (0.5 orders per live model per month) has no source. Base: 12 new models per month (about 54 h/month of measuring, CAD, test prints), 468 orders at $20 = $9,360 revenue; variable cost about $6.30 per order (marketplace fee on $25 incl. $5 shipping about $3.80, material and packaging $1.50, refunds $1.00); fixed $2,060 (two printers $900, spares $200, calipers $60, insurance $600, registration $150, photo and packing $150); cost $5,008; profit about $4,352, roughly $5 per owner hour over about 850 h. Pessimistic (price $16, 234 orders, cost x1.5): revenue $3,744, cost about $5,040, profit about -$1,296. Break-even at the pessimistic price and cost is about 400 orders per year, i.e. about 0.43 orders per live model per month, so the idea needs at least the base-case demand to work. Valuing the owner's time at $10/h makes the base case about -$4.1k.
